subject: Issue resetting arrival times between each rep

messages.author: 828433663124ca03
messages.subject: Issue resetting arrival times between each rep
parts:
I am modeling a hair salon where the arrival rates vary by hour.  I have written a function helper function that outputs a dataframe(sched) of entities whose inter arrival times reflect those varying rates.  

I use the schedule with a generator with this code - 

add_generator("customer", t0, function() sched$IAT[(get_n_generated(envs, "customer")) + 1] , mon = 2)

I tried to replicate using lapply, with this code - 

envsRep <- lapply(1:reps, function(i) {
        sched <- schedIt() #makes the IATs
        envs %>% run(until=730)
})

My intention is to have a new schedule generate at each replication.  However the arrival data shows each replication having the same arrival times - clearly implying that the generator is not 'resetting' when the sched object is recreated.  

Is there a way to make this work? All ideas appreciated.

--

messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Issue resetting arrival times between each rep
parts:
If arrivals are driven by an exponential distribution, this is "memoryless". I.e., you could draw arrivals based on this, then at some point redraw events that haven't occurred yet. So, one could have an event occurring on a set time that triggers a redraw. If the rates change at that point, it works out fine.

I'm driving our simulations via a main event loop. See: https://github.com/spgarbet/right/blob/master/simvastatin/simvastatin.R

This works since most of our events are exponential in our models.

messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Issue resetting arrival times between each rep
parts:
My approach is based on exponential draws, but as it is a non-stationary process the rate (and mean of the exp dist) changes each hour to best match the real world data on clientele - ie I need on average the same number of arrivals per hour that the store did. I addressed this by drawing across the whole sim time at the highest rate, and then thinning the the remaining hours (code below).  The goal here is to have the right number of people arriving in each hour - this can't easily be accomplished by changing the rate on the hour as it is possible to skip part of the busy period.  I'm definitely interested in an example that makes this work however.  

I confess that I don't fully understand what you mean by main event loop.  I also see only the one generator in your code which appears to be regular.

Is it possible to reset the generator between replications?

schedIt <- function() {
        
        ##Here is where you can do a given day or month etc
        ##It is now the average by hour irrespectice of day
        rates <- byHour
        
        rates <- rbind(rates[12,], rates[1:11,]) #gets things in the right order - 10 am was at the end for some reaosn
        maxRate <- max(rates$clients)
        
        ##Make a lot first - ~100 hours worth
        denseGen <- rexp(12000,rate=(1/maxRate))
        
        ##Converts IAT into time of day
        clockSched <- as.numeric()
        temp <- 0
        for(i in 1:length(denseGen)) {
                clockSched <- c(clockSched, temp+denseGen[i])
                temp <- temp+denseGen[i]
        }
        
        ##Takes only the ones that happen before closing
        clockSched <- clockSched[clockSched < 720]
        
        ##'Thins' the values to match the probalities by hour
        rem <- as.numeric()
        startTime <- 0
        endTime <- 60
        for(hour in 1:nrow(rates)) {
                rate <- rates$clients[hour]
                #print(rate)
                for(i in 1:length(clockSched)) {
                        #print(i)
                        test <- runif(1,0:1) > rate/maxRate
                        #print(test)
                        if(clockSched[i] >= startTime & clockSched[i] < endTime) {
                                if(test){rem <- c(rem,i) } }
                        
                }
                startTime <- startTime + 60 
                endTime <- endTime + 60
        }
        
        ##Removes the values from the clock schedule
        clockSched <- clockSched[-rem]
        
        ##converts the clock time back to an updated IAT after 'thinning'
        temp <- 0
        IAT <- as.numeric()
        for(i in 1:length(clockSched)){
                IAT <- c(IAT,clockSched[i]-temp)
                temp <- clockSched[i]
        }
        
        ##Bookkeeping to make a data frame
        id <- seq(1,length(clockSched))
        sched <- cbind(id,clockSched,IAT)  
        sched <- data.frame(sched)
        
        return(sched)
        
}

parts: Check out the introductory vignette, replication section. In your lapply, you are running the same simulator multiple times, but you want multiple simulators (multiple replicas), so you need to embed the whole simulator’s definition inside this lapply. Something like this should do the trick:

envsRep <- lapply(1:reps, function(i) {
  sched <- schedIt() #makes the IATs

env %>% simmer() %>%
    ... 
    add_generator("customer", t0, function() sched$IAT[(get_n_generated(env, "customer")) + 1] , mon = 2)
  env %>% run(until=730)
})
​

messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Issue resetting arrival times between each rep
parts:
If it's arrivals, Iñaki snippet shows the way.

It helps to understand the relationship between exponential distribution and Poisson processes.

First the memoryless property demonstration:

> x <- rexp(1000)
> y <- x
> n <- length(y[x > 1])
> y[x > 1] <- rexp(n) + 1
> hist(x)
> hist(y)

x is a random exponential draw.
y is a redraw for all events that are greater than 1.

When plotted, there is little difference between the two. A ks.test shouldn't be able to tell the difference (if it does it's a type I error). 

So, let's say you're going to simulate 3 hours.

During hour 1, 10 people arrive, or 10 per hour
During hour 2, 50 people arrive, or 50 per hour
During hour 3, 20 people arrive, or 20 per hour.

Generating on demand as Iñaki shows will work, but one must be careful with the borders.

The naive approach ignoring the borders would be as follows:

new_rate <- function(sim_t)
{
  if(sim_t <= 1.0) rexp(1, 10)
  else if(sim_t <= 2.0) rexp(1, 50)
  else if(sim_t <= 3.0) rexp(1, 20)
  else stop("out of sim range")
}

With this a draw at sim_t 0.99 would overlap the 10 per hour rate into hour 2. With a very slow rate transitioning to a fast one, this could impact the simulation. So a little more caution is required with boundary conditions:

new_rate <- function(sim_t)
{
   draw <- if(sim_t <= 1.0) rexp(1, 10)
                else if(sim_t <= 2.0) rexp(1, 50)
                else if(sim_t <= 3.0) rexp(1, 20)
                else stop("out of sim range")

  # Boundary checks
  if(sim_t <= 1.0 && sim_t + draw > 1.0) draw <- sim_t + rexp(1, 50)
  if(sim_t >= 1.0 && sim_t <= 2.0 && sim_t+draw > 2.0) draw <- sim_t + rexp(1,20)
  if(draw > 3.0) draw <- (-1)  # No more

  draw
}

This properly shifts the rates at the boundary, using the memoryless property of the exponential distribution.

        maxRate <- max(rates$clients)
        
        ##Make a lot first - ~100 hours worth
        denseGen <- rexp(12000,rate=(1/maxRate))
        
        ##Converts IAT into time of day
        clockSched <- as.numeric()
        temp <- 0
        for(i in 1:length(denseGen)) {
                clockSched <- c(clockSched, temp+denseGen[i])
                temp <- temp+denseGen[i]
        }
        
        ##Takes only the ones that happen before closing
        clockSched <- clockSched[clockSched < 720]
        
        ##'Thins' the values to match the probalities by hour
        rem <- as.numeric()
        startTime <- 0
        endTime <- 60
        for(hour in 1:nrow(rates)) {
                rate <- rates$clients[hour]
                #print(rate)
                for(i in 1:length(clockSched)) {
                        #print(i)
                        test <- runif(1,0:1) > rate/maxRate
                        #print(test)
                        if(clockSched[i] >= startTime & clockSched[i] < endTime) {
                                if(test){rem <- c(rem,i) } }
                        
                }
                startTime <- startTime + 60 
                endTime <- endTime + 60
        }
        
        ##Removes the values from the clock schedule
        clockSched <- clockSched[-rem]
        
        ##converts the clock time back to an updated IAT after 'thinning'
        temp <- 0
        IAT <- as.numeric()
        for(i in 1:length(clockSched)){
                IAT <- c(IAT,clockSched[i]-temp)
                temp <- clockSched[i]
        }
        
        ##Bookkeeping to make a data frame
        id <- seq(1,length(clockSched))
        sched <- cbind(id,clockSched,IAT)  
        sched <- data.frame(sched)
        
        return(sched)
        
}


On Sat, Jun 4, 2016 at 1:59 PM, Shawn Garbett <shawn....@gmail.com> wrote:
If arrivals are driven by an exponential distribution, this is "memoryless". I.e., you could draw arrivals based on this, then at some point redraw events that haven't occurred yet. So, one could have an event occurring on a set time that triggers a redraw. If the rates change at that point, it works out fine.

I'm driving our simulations via a main event loop. See: https://github.com/spgarbet/right/blob/master/simvastatin/simvastatin.R

This works since most of our events are exponential in our models.

parts: Just realized I got it wrong. Boundaries are tricky! I think this is what was intended....

new_rate <- function(sim_t)
{
   draw <- if(sim_t <= 1.0) rexp(1, 10)
                else if(sim_t <= 2.0) rexp(1, 50)
                else if(sim_t <= 3.0) rexp(1, 20)
                else stop("out of sim range")

  # Boundary checks

if(sim_t <= 1.0 && sim_t + draw > 1.0) draw <- (1.0 - sim_t) + rexp(1, 50)
  if(sim_t >= 1.0 && sim_t <= 2.0 && sim_t+draw > 2.0) draw <- (2.0 - sim_t) + rexp(1,20)

if(draw > 3.0) draw <- (-1)  # No more

  draw
}
